# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Attorney]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 27, 2026
**Re:** Mibaix Marine Systems LLC / Bupaiv Ballast Technologies Ltd.: Review of Distribution Arrangement Documents

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed all six documents in the folder:

- **Distribution Agreement** dated March 3, 2025 (the "DA")
- **Statement of Work No. 1** dated June 16, 2025 (the "SOW")
- **Amendment No. 1** dated September 15, 2026 (the "Amendment")
- **Parent Company Guaranty** from Mibaix Holdings Corp. dated September 15, 2026 (the "Guaranty")
- **Broker's insurance certificate cover letter** dated October 6, 2026
- **Q4 2026 rolling purchase forecast** dated October 14, 2026

Mibaix is Bupaiv's exclusive distributor for a **Territory consisting of the U.S. Gulf Coast ports of Houston, New Orleans, Mobile and Corpus Christi** (DA §1.1). The Initial Term is five years from March 3, 2025 (DA §2.1). The DA, the SOW and the Amendment are governed by New York law, with exclusive jurisdiction in the state and federal courts in New York County (DA §§19.1–19.2; SOW §12.1; Amendment §8.3).

I found six issues that materially affect Mibaix. They are listed below in priority order. The most urgent is the pending parent-level sale to Nordhaven. It is time-critical because closing is expected in Q1 2027, and it puts the entire distributorship at risk. If the distributorship is terminated, the overbroad post-term non-compete would then take effect.

| # | Priority | Issue | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Critical / urgent** | Pending Nordhaven sale of parent triggers Bupaiv's change-of-control termination right; no consent on file | DA §17.2, §21.5; Guaranty Recital B |
| 2 | **High** | Mibaix's installation indemnity for Environmental Claims is uncapped | DA §11.3(a), §11.2; SOW §6.2 |
| 3 | **High** | Amendment silently drops spare parts and consumables from "Products" | Amendment §2.1; DA §1.1 |
| 4 | **High** | Worldwide, 24-month post-term non-compete covering scrubbers and Mibaix's existing business | DA §3.4 |
| 5 | **Medium–High** | "Affiliate" definition lets Bupaiv assign to a competing distributor without consent | DA §20.1; DA §1.1 ("Affiliate") |
| 6 | **Medium** | Guaranty governed by English law and English courts, out of step with the DA's New York law and forum | Guaranty §14; DA §§19.1–19.2 |

The insurance cover letter and the purchase forecast do not raise independent legal issues. Where they bear on the issues above, I have relied on them for context.

---

## 2. Issues (in priority order)

### Issue 1: Pending sale of Mibaix Holdings to Nordhaven is a Change of Control that lets Bupaiv terminate (CRITICAL / URGENT)

**Where it appears:**
- Distribution Agreement §17.2 (Change of Control) and §21.5 (Waiver)
- Parent Guaranty, Recital B

**What the documents say:**
- **The termination right.** DA §17.2 lets Bupaiv terminate on 90 days' notice "if a Change of Control of Distributor occurs without Supplier's prior written consent."
- **The definition.** "Change of Control" expressly includes acquisition of more than 50% of the voting securities "of Distributor **or of any entity that directly or indirectly controls Distributor**."
- **The pending deal.** Guaranty Recital B records two facts:
  - Mibaix Holdings Corp. owns 100% of Mibaix.
  - Mibaix Holdings has signed a share purchase agreement dated August 28, 2026 under which Nordhaven Maritime Group plc will acquire all of its shares, with closing expected in Q1 2027.
- **The result.** This is squarely a Change of Control of the Distributor. The fact that the sale happens at the parent level does not take it outside the definition, because the definition reaches indirect control.

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- **No consent on file.** Nothing in the folder records Bupaiv's prior written consent. That includes Amendment No. 1, which Bupaiv signed the same day the Guaranty disclosed the sale.
- **Knowledge is not consent.** Bupaiv plainly knows of the deal. But DA §21.5 provides that Supplier's knowledge of "any proposed or completed transaction affecting the ownership of Distributor" is not consent or waiver. Mibaix therefore cannot argue implied consent or waiver from Bupaiv's countersignature of the Guaranty or the Amendment.
- **Long exercise window.** Bupaiv may serve notice at any time within 12 months after it first learns of the Change of Control. It could hold the termination right over Mibaix well into 2027–2028 as leverage on pricing, minimums or other terms.
- **Consequences of termination:**
  - Mibaix loses its exclusive Territory and the BX-900 launch.
  - Its forecast pipeline is at risk: 26 units, about US$11.85 million, for 2027.
  - The 24-month worldwide non-compete in DA §3.4 would take effect (see Issue 4).
  - Termination would also likely reduce the value of the Nordhaven transaction itself.
- **Separate notice duty.** DA §17.2 also requires Mibaix to give written notice of any proposed Change of Control as soon as permitted. Mibaix should confirm it has done so formally, under DA §21.1, and not only through the Guaranty recital.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Before closing, obtain Bupaiv's written consent to the Nordhaven transaction. The consent should:
   - be signed by an authorized Bupaiv representative;
   - refer expressly to the August 28, 2026 SPA; and
   - waive the §17.2 termination right for that transaction.
   Ideally, document it as a short amendment or consent letter under DA §21.2.
2. Coordinate with the parent's deal counsel. Bupaiv's consent should be a closing condition or a covenant in the SPA, and the sale should not close without it.
3. Serve formal written notice of the proposed Change of Control under DA §§17.2 and 21.1, if this has not already been done.
4. In any renegotiation, seek to:
   - narrow §17.2 to exclude transfers to non-competitors; or
   - require that Bupaiv's consent not be unreasonably withheld.

---

### Issue 2: Mibaix's installation indemnity for Environmental Claims is uncapped (HIGH)

**Where it appears:**
- Distribution Agreement §11.3(a), read with §11.2 and §1.1 ("Environmental Claim")
- SOW No. 1 §6.2

**What the documents say:**
- **The cap.** DA §11.2 caps each Party's aggregate liability under the Agreement "and any Statement of Work" at the amounts Mibaix paid Bupaiv in the preceding 12 months.
- **The carve-out.** DA §11.3(a) removes from both the cap and the consequential-damages exclusion (§11.1) all "indemnification obligations with respect to Environmental Claims."
- **The definition.** "Environmental Claim" is defined broadly as "any claim, fine or penalty arising from a discharge of ballast water or treatment residuals" (DA §1.1).
- **Within the DA alone, the carve-out favours Mibaix.** The only Environmental Claims indemnity in the DA is Bupaiv's product-defect indemnity in §10.2.
- **The SOW adds a Mibaix indemnity.** SOW §6.2 requires Mibaix to "indemnify, defend and hold harmless Supplier" against all Losses from any Environmental Claim "arising out of or relating to the Installation Services."
- **"Subject to Section 11" does not cap it.** That phrase reads like an ordinary capped indemnity. But Section 11 includes the §11.3(a) carve-out. Applying Section 11 as written therefore removes the cap from this indemnity.
- **Precedence does not help.** The DA §21.3 order of precedence does not assist, because the SOW and the DA do not conflict. They operate together.

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- **Unlimited exposure.** Mibaix has unlimited liability to Bupaiv for ballast-water and treatment-residual discharge claims, fines and penalties connected with its installation work. This includes exposure under the Clean Water Act, VIDA and the Coast Guard rules at 33 C.F.R. Part 151, all of which are incorporated into "Applicable Law" (DA §1.1).
- **Consequential losses too.** Because §11.3 also lifts the §11.1 exclusion, Bupaiv could recover consequential losses through this indemnity.
- **Broad trigger.** The "arising out of or relating to" language is wide. Commissioning itself requires Mibaix to run a treatment cycle and a discharge cycle (SOW §3.4(d)). Bupaiv could argue that any discharge exceedance after Mibaix commissions a unit "relates to" the Installation Services, even if the true cause is a product issue. That would push liability back onto Mibaix and blunt Bupaiv's own §10.2 indemnity.
- **Likely insurance gap.** DA §14.2 does not require Mibaix to carry pollution liability insurance, and the broker's October 6, 2026 summary lists no pollution or environmental liability cover. Bupaiv, by contrast, must carry US$10 million of marine pollution cover (DA §14.1(b)). Mibaix's uncapped exposure therefore appears to be largely uninsured.
- **Wide reach.** SOW Jobs include Reserved Account retrofits and warranty and recall work. The forecast expects three Reserved Account jobs in 2027.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend DA §11.3(a) so the carve-out applies only to "Supplier's obligations under Section 10.2."
2. Alternatively, amend SOW §6.2 to state expressly that Mibaix's liability under it "is subject to the cap in Section 11.2 and the exclusion in Section 11.1, notwithstanding Section 11.3(a)."
3. In either case, also:
   - narrow the SOW §6.2 trigger to Environmental Claims "to the extent caused by Distributor's negligent or non-conforming performance of the Installation Services";
   - exclude claims caused by a Defect, by Supplier's drawings or instructions, or by crew operation (consistent with SOW §8.3); and
   - add an express statement that Bupaiv's §10.2 indemnity takes priority where a Defect contributes to the discharge.
4. Separately, ask the broker to quote contractor's pollution liability cover.

---

### Issue 3: Amendment No. 1 redefines "Products" and drops spare parts and consumables (HIGH)

**Where it appears:**
- Amendment No. 1 §2.1
- Distribution Agreement §1.1 ("Products") and Schedule A, Part 2

**What the documents say:**
- **Original definition.** The DA defined "Products" as "the BWTS units, spare parts and consumables listed in Schedule A." Schedule A, Part 2 lists ten categories of spare parts and consumables.
- **New definition.** Amendment §2.1 is presented in the recitals as simply adding the BX-900. It actually deletes the definition "in its entirety" and replaces it with "the ballast water treatment system models listed in Part 1 of Schedule A." Spare parts and consumables are silently dropped.
- **The Amendment controls.** Under DA §21.3, Amendments prevail over the DA. Amendment §8.1 also makes the Amendment part of the Agreement from September 15, 2026.

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- **Exclusivity (DA §3.1).** Mibaix is no longer the exclusive distributor of parts and consumables. Bupaiv can appoint others, or sell directly into the Territory, for the aftermarket on Mibaix's installed base of 31 units.
- **Warranty (DA §12).** Section 12.1 warrants each "Product." Spare parts and consumables arguably lose warranty cover, even though §12.2(b)–(c) still set warranty periods for them. The Amendment preserves warranties expressly only for BX-900 units (Amendment §7.2). Mibaix's pass-through of warranties to its Customers (§12.5) is affected in the same way.
- **Minimum Annual Purchase.** Only "Products" count toward the minimum (DA §§5.1–5.2). Parts and consumables purchases, which the forecast puts at about US$412,000 for 2027, no longer count toward the raised US$6,200,000 Minimum Annual Purchase that applies from March 3, 2027 (Amendment §§3.1–3.2). That raises the shortfall risk, and with it the risk that Bupaiv converts the appointment to non-exclusive under §5.3.
- **Pricing and other protections.** These also run off "Products" and may no longer apply to parts:
  - the most-favoured-pricing clause (§6.4);
  - capacity commitments (§5.5);
  - recall cost coverage (§13.5); and
  - post-termination repurchase (§17.5(c)).
- **Non-compete exposure.** DA §3.4 bars Mibaix from distributing or servicing ballast water treatment equipment "other than Products." Reselling Bupaiv's own spare parts and consumables may now fall within the non-compete and could be argued to be a breach.
- **Pricing mechanics.** Schedule B, Part 2, which sets the 32% parts discount, remains in place, but it now prices items that are outside the defined term.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Execute a corrective amendment under DA §21.2 restoring the original definition and adding the BX-900. Suggested wording: "Products" means the BWTS units listed in Part 1 of Schedule A (including the BX-900) and the spare parts and consumables listed in Part 2 of Schedule A.
2. Expressly add BX-900 parts and consumables to Schedule A, Part 2 once Bupaiv publishes them (the forecast, §8.3, notes they are still outstanding).
3. Make the corrective amendment effective retroactively to September 15, 2026, and confirm that parts purchases since then count toward the Minimum Annual Purchase.
4. Pending execution, obtain Bupaiv's written confirmation that it was not intended to change the scope of Products.

---

### Issue 4: Overbroad worldwide, post-term non-compete covering scrubbers and Mibaix's existing business (HIGH)

**Where it appears:** Distribution Agreement §3.4 (survives termination under §17.7).

**What the documents say:**
- **Scope of the restraint.** During the Term and for **twenty-four (24) months after** expiration or termination, Mibaix may not manufacture, distribute, sell, market or service "any ballast water treatment, **exhaust gas scrubber or other marine environmental compliance equipment** other than Products, **anywhere in the world**." Mibaix also may not hold an interest in, or act as agent or consultant for, anyone engaged in those activities.
- **Scope of the deal.** Mibaix's appointment covers only the four Gulf Coast ports in the Territory (DA §1.1).
- **Existing business.** DA Recital B acknowledges that Mibaix "currently operates an exhaust gas scrubber servicing business at Gulf and Caribbean ports."

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- **It bars Mibaix's existing business.** Read literally, the covenant prohibits Mibaix's scrubber servicing business now, during the Term. There is no carve-out for that business, despite the recital. Bupaiv could treat continued scrubber work as a material breach under §17.1, giving it a termination lever and a damages claim.
- **It reaches unrelated markets.** It goes well beyond what Bupaiv needs to protect its Territory exclusivity. It covers:
  - product lines Bupaiv does not make (scrubbers, other compliance equipment); and
  - geographies Mibaix was never appointed for (the whole world, including the Caribbean ports where Mibaix already operates).
- **It blocks common aftermarket work.** It prohibits servicing third-party BWTS. The forecast (§2.2(c)) shows replacement demand from operators with other manufacturers' systems, which is a common source of service and retrofit work.
- **Post-term effect.** After termination, including a termination for change of control under Issue 1, Mibaix would be locked out of its core markets worldwide for two years.
- **Enforceability does not remove the risk.** New York applies a reasonableness test to restrictive covenants. A restraint must be no greater than needed to protect a legitimate interest, must not impose undue hardship, and must not harm the public. A worldwide, multi-product covenant extending to the client's pre-existing business is vulnerable under that test. But New York courts may partially enforce (blue-pencil) an overbroad covenant, and until a court rules the clause chills Mibaix's operations and gives Bupaiv leverage.
- **Interaction with Issue 3.** With "Products" now narrowed, reselling Bupaiv's own parts may be caught by the covenant as well.

**Recommended fix:** Narrow §3.4 so that it:
- covers only ballast water treatment systems **competing with the Products**;
- applies only **within the Territory**;
- applies only **during the Term**, with no post-term tail, or at most a short tail (e.g., 6 months) that does not apply where Bupaiv terminates without cause or for change of control;
- **expressly carves out** Mibaix's existing and future exhaust gas scrubber business and other non-BWTS environmental compliance work, wherever conducted;
- carves out servicing of third-party BWTS already installed on Customer vessels; and
- carves out passive investments (e.g., under 5% of a listed company).

Pending renegotiation, get a written acknowledgment from Bupaiv that Mibaix's scrubber business does not breach §3.4.

---

### Issue 5: "Affiliate" definition lets Bupaiv assign the Agreement to a competing distributor without consent (MEDIUM–HIGH)

**Where it appears:** Distribution Agreement §20.1, read with the "Affiliate" definition in §1.1.

**What the documents say:**
- **The assignment clause looks mutual.** Section 20.1 bars assignment without consent, "except that either Party may assign this Agreement in whole **to an Affiliate without such consent** by giving written notice."
- **But "Affiliate" is defined very broadly.** It covers entities under common control and also "any entity with which that Party has a commercial alliance, joint venture or **distribution relationship**."

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- **Bupaiv can assign to a rival.** Bupaiv is a manufacturer with distribution relationships worldwide. It could assign the Agreement, without Mibaix's consent, to any of its other distributors, including a Gulf Coast competitor of Mibaix.
- **Mibaix's confidential data would follow.** The assignee would take Bupaiv's rights to Mibaix's confidential pricing, Customer lists, vessel data, commissioning records (DA §8.4) and forecasts. The Q4 2026 forecast alone discloses Customer opportunities by port and confidence grade.
- **The guaranty would follow too.** Bupaiv can assign the Guaranty together with any permitted assignment of the Agreement (Guaranty §15.2), so the parent's guaranty could also pass to a competitor.
- **Confidentiality leak.** The same broad definition applies to the confidentiality carve-out in DA §15.3(b). Bupaiv can share Mibaix's Confidential Information with its "Affiliates'" employees and advisers, which includes its other distributors.
- **The exception is one-sided in practice.** Mibaix has little practical use for it. Meanwhile, the DA restricts only Mibaix's change of control (§17.2), not Bupaiv's.
- **Narrower definitions elsewhere.** The DA already uses a narrower concept in places ("Affiliates under common control," §§10.1–10.2), which shows the broad definition is not needed.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Limit "Affiliate" to entities that control, are controlled by, or are under common control with a Party. Delete "commercial alliance, joint venture or distribution relationship."
2. In §20.1, prohibit any assignment, including to an Affiliate, to a person that competes with Distributor in the Territory or distributes BWTS in the Territory.
3. Require that any assignee assume all obligations in writing and that the assignor remain liable.
4. Add a reciprocal change-of-control right for Mibaix if Bupaiv is acquired by, or its business transferred to, a competitor of Mibaix.
5. Conform the confidentiality carve-out in DA §15.3(b) to the narrowed definition.

---

### Issue 6: Parent Guaranty is governed by English law with exclusive English courts, out of step with the DA's New York law and forum (MEDIUM)

**Where it appears:**
- Parent Guaranty §14 (§§14.1–14.3)
- Distribution Agreement §§19.1–19.2

**What the documents say:**
- **The Guaranty.** It is governed by "the laws of England and Wales," and "the courts of England and Wales have exclusive jurisdiction" over any dispute arising out of or in connection with it. The Guarantor has appointed a London process agent (§14.3).
- **The DA.** The guaranteed obligations under the DA (and each SOW) are governed by New York law. Disputes go exclusively to the state and federal courts in New York County (DA §§19.1–19.2).
- **No reconciliation mechanism.** The DA §21.3 precedence clause covers only Amendments, the DA and Statements of Work. It does not reach the Guaranty and cannot reconcile the two regimes.

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- **Parallel proceedings.** Bupaiv could sue Mibaix Holdings in London under English guarantee law while Mibaix's defences to the underlying debt are decided in New York. Those defences include good-faith invoice disputes, set-off under SOW §7.5, and liquidated damages for late delivery. That creates a real risk of inconsistent results.
- **Defences tried in the wrong forum.** Guaranty §2.4 lets the Guarantor raise the Distributor's defences. But they would be tried in an English court applying New York law to the DA, which adds cost, delay and the need for expert evidence. Mibaix itself, as a non-party to the Guaranty, could not easily join.
- **Burden on the client group.** The parent, a Houston-based Delaware corporation, bears the cost of foreign litigation and the risk of an English judgment enforceable against its U.S. assets.
- **Exposure is significant.** The guaranty extends to up to US$2.5 million of Product price at any one time, plus interest and costs (Guaranty §5.2).
- **It may survive the sale.** The Guaranty survives changes in ownership (§5.1(d)), so these terms will likely bind the parent after the Nordhaven sale.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend Guaranty §14 under Guaranty §16.1 to provide for:
   - New York governing law;
   - exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County, matching DA §19.2; and
   - removal of the London process agent requirement.
2. Fallback position: make the English jurisdiction non-exclusive, and require Bupaiv to stay any Guaranty claim while a dispute over the underlying obligation is pending in New York. A determination in the New York proceeding would then bind the Guaranty claim.
3. Consider making this change part of the same consent and amendment package proposed for Issues 1 and 3.

---

## 3. Other Documents Reviewed

- **Insurance certificate cover letter (October 6, 2026).** The broker's summary shows that Mibaix's renewed program meets the DA §14.2 requirements (CGL, ship repairer's legal liability, USL&H/workers' compensation, auto). It raises no contractual issue on its own. It does show no pollution liability cover, which matters to Issue 2. The letter itself notes it is not a legal opinion and that the certificates and endorsements control.
- **Q4 2026 purchase forecast (October 14, 2026).** The forecast is non-binding (DA §5.4) and appears consistent with the Amendment's lead time, credit-note and Minimum Annual Purchase provisions. It is useful context for three issues:
  - Issue 1: the value at stake is about US$11.85 million of forecast 2027 BWTS purchases.
  - Issue 3: about US$412,000 of parts and consumables now falls outside "Products," and the §9 Minimum Annual Purchase tracking counts only BWTS units.
  - Issue 4: the forecast refers to demand from operators of third-party systems.

---

## 4. Recommended Next Steps

1. **Immediately:** Contact the parent's M&A counsel. Seek Bupaiv's written consent to the Nordhaven transaction, with a waiver of DA §17.2, as a pre-closing deliverable (Issue 1).
2. **Package the remaining fixes** into a single Amendment No. 2 and Guaranty amendment, negotiated alongside the consent request. It should cover:
   - the Environmental Claims cap carve-out (Issue 2);
   - restoring parts and consumables to "Products" (Issue 3);
   - narrowing the non-compete and carving out the scrubber business (Issue 4);
   - narrowing "Affiliate" and prohibiting assignment to competitors (Issue 5); and
   - conforming the Guaranty to New York law and forum (Issue 6).
3. **Interim protections:** Obtain written confirmations from Bupaiv on:
   - the scope of Products; and
   - the scrubber business not breaching §3.4.
4. **Insurance:** Ask the broker to quote contractor's pollution liability cover while Issue 2 is being negotiated.

Please let me know if you would like draft amendment language for any of these points.

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- Within the Agreement itself, the only Environmental Claims indemnity is Supplier's product-defect indemnity in § 10.2, so the § 11.3(a) carve-out appears to favor Mibaix.
- SOW § 6.2 creates a second Environmental Claims indemnity, given by Mibaix. The words "subject to Section 11" look like a cap, but Section 11 includes § 11.3(a). That clause takes this indemnity outside both the cap and the consequential-damages waiver.

- The result is that Mibaix has **unlimited** exposure to Bupaiv for ballast-discharge fines, penalties and third-party claims "arising out of or relating to" installation and commissioning. This could include Clean Water Act penalties, U.S. Coast Guard enforcement under 33 C.F.R. Part 151, and VIDA claims.
- The "relating to" wording is broad. It could capture discharges during commissioning treatment and discharge cycles (SOW § 3.4(d)) even where the root cause is a disputed product issue.
- The broker letter shows commercial general liability and ship repairer's liability limits of US$5 million. It does not show pollution coverage for Mibaix, so this exposure is likely uninsured.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend Agreement § 11.3(a) so that it reads "**Supplier's** indemnification obligations under Section 10.2 with respect to Environmental Claims."
- Alternatively, amend SOW § 6.2 so that it is expressly "subject to the cap in Section 11.2 of the Agreement, notwithstanding Section 11.3(a)."
- In either case:
  - narrow § 6.2 to Environmental Claims "to the extent caused by the negligence or willful misconduct of Distributor or its subcontractors";
  - exclude claims caused by a Defect or by Supplier's drawings and instructions, consistent with SOW § 8.3; and
  - coordinate with the broker on pollution liability coverage.

### Issue 3: Amendment No. 1 Silently Removes Spare Parts and Consumables from "Products" (High)

**Where:** Amendment § 2.1, against Agreement § 1.1 ("Products"). See also Agreement § 21.3, Amendment § 8.1, and Agreement Schedule A Part 2.

**What the documents say:**
- Agreement § 1.1 defines "Products" as "the BWTS units, spare parts and consumables listed in Schedule A." Schedule A Part 2 lists UV lamps, quartz sleeves, filter elements, PLC modules, CIP fluid, calibration kits and similar items.
- The Amendment is presented as adding the BX-900. Section 2.1, however, deletes the whole definition and replaces it with: "the ballast water treatment system models listed in Part 1 of Schedule A." Part 2 is not mentioned.
- Under Agreement § 21.3, Amendments prevail over the Agreement.

**Why it matters for Mibaix:** Because "Products" drives most of the Agreement, removing parts and consumables has wide effects:
- **Exclusivity (§ 3.1).** Mibaix loses exclusivity for parts and consumables. Bupaiv could appoint other parts resellers in the Territory or sell aftermarket parts directly to Mibaix's installed-base customers. The forecast puts that installed base at 31 units.
- **Warranty (§ 12).** The § 12.1 warranties and the § 12.2(b)–(c) warranty periods for spare parts and consumables arguably fall away, together with the § 12.4 labor reimbursement and the § 12.5 customer pass-through.
- **Minimum Annual Purchase (§§ 5.1–5.2).** The minimum rises to US$6,200,000 from March 3, 2027 (Amendment §§ 3.1–3.2). Parts and consumables purchases would no longer count toward it, so roughly US$412,000 per year of forecast purchases would provide no credit.
- **Other provisions.** Pricing (Schedule B Part 2 discount of 32%), most-favored pricing (§ 6.4), inspection and replacement (§ 7.4), recalls (§ 13.5), the IP indemnity (§ 10.3) and the post-termination parts supply in § 17.5(d) are all tied to "Products." Their application to parts becomes doubtful.
- **Ordering.** It is unclear under what terms Mibaix may continue to order parts at all. That uncertainty undercuts its servicing business and the forecast in Section 8.

Amendment § 8.1 ("[e]xcept as expressly amended … the Agreement remains unchanged") does not cure the problem, because the definition *was* expressly replaced.

**Recommended fix:**
- Execute a short corrective amendment under § 21.2 that restores the original definition with the BX-900 added. Suggested wording: "'Products' means the BWTS units (including the BX-900), spare parts and consumables listed in Schedule A, as amended from time to time."
- Confirm that Schedule A Part 2 remains in force and covers BX-900 parts.
- State that the correction applies retroactively from the Amendment Effective Date, so there is no gap in exclusivity, warranty or minimum-purchase credit.

### Issue 4: The "Affiliate" Definition Lets Bupaiv Assign to a Competing Distributor Without Consent (Medium-High)

**Where:** Agreement § 1.1 ("Affiliate") and § 20.1 (Assignment). See also Guaranty § 15.2.

**What the documents say:**
- Section 20.1 prohibits assignment without consent, "except that either Party may assign this Agreement in whole to an Affiliate without such consent."
- Section 1.1 defines "Affiliate" to include not only entities under common control but also "any entity with which that Party has a commercial alliance, joint venture or distribution relationship."

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- Bupaiv is a manufacturer with distribution relationships around the world. Each of its distributors is an "Affiliate" of Bupaiv, so Bupaiv could assign the entire Agreement, without Mibaix's consent, to any of them, including a direct Gulf Coast competitor of Mibaix.
- The assignee would step into Bupaiv's position. It would receive Mibaix's Confidential Information (pricing, customer lists, vessel data and forecasts, as defined in § 15.1) and control Mibaix's supply.
- Under Guaranty § 15.2 the Guaranty would follow the assignment, so the assignee would also hold Holdings' guaranty.
- The exception gives Mibaix little of real value in return.
- The Agreement restricts only the Distributor's change of control (§ 17.2), not the Supplier's, so Mibaix has no protection at the Supplier level either.

**Recommended fix:**
- Limit "Affiliate" to entities that control, are controlled by, or are under common control with a Party, and delete "commercial alliance, joint venture or distribution relationship."
- If a broader concept is needed elsewhere, use a separate defined term.
- Add an express prohibition on any assignment by Supplier to a person that distributes, sells or services ballast water treatment systems in the Territory.
- Consider a reciprocal right for Mibaix to terminate if Supplier undergoes a change of control.

### Issue 5: Guaranty Is Governed by English Law with Exclusive English Courts (Medium)

**Where:** Guaranty § 14 (§§ 14.1–14.3), against Agreement §§ 19.1–19.2. See also Agreement § 21.3.

**What the documents say:**
- Guaranty § 14.1 chooses the laws of England and Wales. Section 14.2 gives the courts of England and Wales exclusive jurisdiction, and § 14.3 appoints a London process agent.
- The guaranteed obligations arise under the Agreement, which is governed by New York law with exclusive jurisdiction in the state and federal courts in New York County (§§ 19.1–19.2).
- The order of precedence in Agreement § 21.3 covers only Amendments, the Agreement and SOWs. It does not reach the Guaranty and cannot reconcile the two.

**Why it matters for Mibaix:**
- Bupaiv could sue Holdings in London under English guarantee law while any dispute over the underlying debt between Bupaiv and Distributor proceeds in New York. Examples include a good-faith invoice dispute under § 6.5, or a set-off under SOW § 7.5.
- Guaranty § 2.4 preserves Distributor's defenses for the Guarantor. An English court would nevertheless decide those New York-law defenses separately, which creates a risk of inconsistent results, duplicated cost, and Holdings paying before the New York dispute is resolved.
- The Guaranty is primary-obligor and "payment, not collection" (§§ 2.1–2.2), which increases that risk.
- The pending Nordhaven acquisition makes it more important to get the Guaranty right now, before ownership changes.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend Guaranty § 14 so that it is governed by New York law and subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County, mirroring Agreement §§ 19.1–19.2.
- Add a jury waiver consistent with Agreement § 19.6.
- Delete the London process agent and appoint a New York agent.
- At a minimum, require that any claim against the Guarantor be brought in, or consolidated with, the New York proceeding on the underlying obligation.
